entries.modern_form: Chinese 茶 chá 'tea' (Wade-Giles ch'a; Middle Chinese *ɖˠa, Old Chinese *rlaː), the ultimate source of every 'tea' word in Eurasia
entries.note: The root box is right: the world's tea vocabulary goes back to one Chinese etymon, 茶, whose Mandarin/standard reading is chá (Wade-Giles ch'a, Nourai's 'Č'a'). Nourai's two-branch chart reproduces exactly the split all handbooks make: (a) the chá branch, carried overland along the caravan routes into Persian čāy, Turkish çay, Russian чай, Hindi cāy, Arabic šāy; (b) the Southern-Min (Amoy/Hokkien) branch tê, carried by sea by the Dutch East India Company from 1610 and giving Malay teh, Dutch thee, French thé, German Tee, Italian tè, English tea. Hobson-Jobson makes the same division explicitly. The only defect on the page is the printed form of the southern word, 't'a' for t'e (see node #2). The gloss 'tea' and the language label 'Chinese' are correct; strictly the label for the root is Mandarin/standard Chinese and for node #2 Southern Min, but the book has no finer labels.
entries.note_fa: جعبهٔ ریشه درست است: همهٔ واژه‌های «چای» در اوراسیا به یک واژهٔ چینی، 茶، بازمی‌گردد که خوانش معیار (ماندارین) آن chá است — همان «Č'a»ی نورایی. نمودار نورایی دقیقاً همان دوشاخگیِ شناخته‌شده را نشان می‌دهد: شاخهٔ chá که از راه خشکی و جادهٔ ابریشم به فارسی «چای»، ترکی çay، روسی чай، هندی cāy و عربی «شای» رسید؛ و شاخهٔ جنوبیِ مین (لهجهٔ اَموی) tê که از سدهٔ ۱۷ م. با کشتی‌های کمپانی هند شرقیِ هلند به مالایی teh، هلندی thee، فرانسوی thé، آلمانی Tee و انگلیسی tea انجامید. تنها ایراد صفحه، صورت چاپیِ واژهٔ جنوبی است که «t'a» آمده به‌جای t'e (نگاه کنید به گرهٔ ۲). برچسب زبانی و معنای «چای» درست است.

nodes.derivation: Persian چای čāy 'tea' is a loan from the northern/standard Chinese reading chá, not from the southern tê that gave English tea. Tea reached Iran overland from China (Safavid period, 17th c.; it became the everyday drink only in the 19th c., largely through Russian trade), so Persian belongs to the 'chai' isogloss together with Turkish çay, Russian чай, Hindi cāy and Arabic شاي šāy. The final -y of čāy — absent in Chinese chá — is explained two ways: (a) from the Chinese compound 茶葉 cháyè 'tea leaves', the form Lokotsch cites and Wiktionary gives as the likelier source; (b) as a Persian/Turkic suffixation of čā. Mo'in simply tags it مأخوذ از چینی 'taken from Chinese'. Borhan-e Qate' (Mo'in's footnote in vol. 2) notes that the Arabicised forms of چای are «صای» and «شای». The internet claim that čāy comes from the Persian verb چاییدن is folk etymology and has no standing.
nodes.derivation_fa: «چای» وام‌واژه‌ای است از چینیِ معیار chá و نه از صورت جنوبیِ tê که انگلیسی tea از آن آمده است؛ چای از راه خشکی و از چین به ایران رسید (عصر صفوی، سدهٔ ۱۱ ق./۱۷ م.) و از سدهٔ ۱۳ ق./۱۹ م. با بازرگانی روسیه نوشیدنیِ همگانی شد، از این‌رو فارسی در همان دستهٔ «چای» جای می‌گیرد که ترکی çay، روسی чай، هندی cāy و عربی «شای» در آن‌اند. «ی» پایانی که در chá چینی نیست، یا از ترکیبِ چینی 茶葉 (cháyè) «برگ چای» بازمانده است — تبیینی که لوکوچ و ویکی‌واژه می‌پسندند — یا پسوندی است ایرانی/ترکی بر چا. معین در فرهنگ فارسی تنها می‌نویسد «مأخوذ از چینی»، و معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع یادآور می‌شود که معرّبِ چای «صای» و «شای» است. این ادعای رایج که «چای» از مصدر «چاییدن» آمده ریشه‌شناسی عامیانه است و پایه‌ای ندارد. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: The node is right in substance and wrong in its letter. The southern form that fed Malay teh, Dutch thee and English tea is the Southern Min (Amoy/Hokkien, Xiamen) reading of 茶, tê — Wade-Giles t'e, Skeat's 'të', Klein's 'dial. S. Chin. te', AHD's 'Amoy te'. There is no Chinese form t'a: Mandarin has chá, Amoy has tê, and t'a would be neither. The printed page (PDF p. 104, book p. 74) shows 't'a : tea (South Chinese accent)', so the extraction is faithful and the error is the book's own misprint — the more clearly so because Nourai's own cited page, Klein 1578, prints 'te'. Read t'e, the node is confirmed: Amoy tê and Mandarin chá are the same character 茶 in two dialect readings, both from Middle Chinese *ɖˠa, and the coastal Amoy/Xiamen ports were where the first European tea cargoes were loaded.

Chin. te» و فرهنگ American Heritage «Amoy te». صورتی به شکل t'a در چینی وجود ندارد. تصویرِ صفحهٔ چاپی (ص ۷۴ کتاب = ص ۱۰۴ پی‌دی‌اف) خودِ «t'a» را نشان می‌دهد، پس خطای خوانشِ اسکن نیست بلکه خطای چاپیِ کتاب است — به‌ویژه که همان صفحهٔ کلاین که نورایی بدان ارجاع داده (ص ۱۵۷۸) «te» چاپ کرده است. با خواندنِ t'e، گره پذیرفتنی است: tê اَمویی و chá ماندارین دو خوانشِ یک نویسه‌اند و هر دو از چینیِ میانهٔ *ɖˠa می‌آیند، و بندرهای اَموی/شیامن همان‌جایی بودند که نخستین محموله‌های چای اروپا از آنجا بار زده شد.

nodes.derivation: Malay teh 'tea' was taken from Hokkien tê by the large Hokkien trading community of the Malay archipelago; Malay -eh simply spells the mid front vowel of tê. It is the form the Dutch met in Java and Batavia, and AHD, Klein and Hobson-Jobson all put it between Amoy and Dutch exactly as Nourai does. Two small caveats: the language is Malay (Bahasa Melayu), not 'Malaysian' — the modern national standard of Malaysia post-dates the borrowing by three centuries; and Skeat (1911) reverses the arrow, making Malay teh a re-borrowing from European tea, an isolated view not followed by AHD or the OED.
nodes.derivation_fa: مالاییِ teh «چای» از هوکینِ (مینِ جنوبیِ) tê گرفته شده است؛ بازرگانان هوکین‌زبان در جزایر مالایا این واژه را رواج دادند و «‑eh» مالایی تنها املای همان واکهٔ میانیِ پیشینِ tê است. همین صورت بود که هلندی‌ها در جاوه و باتاویا با آن روبه‌رو شدند، و فرهنگ American Heritage و کلاین و هابسن‑جابسن هر سه آن را دقیقاً در همان جایگاهی می‌نشانند که نورایی نشانده است. دو نکتهٔ کوچک: نام درستِ زبان «مالایی» است نه «مالزیایی» — زبان معیارِ کشور مالزی سه سده پس از این وام‌گیری پدید آمد؛ و اسکیت (۱۹۱۱) جهت پیکان را وارونه می‌کند و teh مالایی را وام‌گرفته از صورت‌های اروپایی می‌داند که دیدگاهی تنهاست و پذیرفته نشده. ادعای نورایی در این گره درست است.

nodes.derivation: Dutch thee is the decisive link in the western chain: the Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie shipped tea from Java to Amsterdam from 1610, and from Dutch the word passed into French thé, German Tee, Italian tè, Spanish té and English tea. Dutch <th> here is not a fricative — Dutch has no /θ/ — it is simply a learned/etymologising spelling of /t/, which is why the borrowing surfaces as plain t- in French and English. Etymonline states the reason for the Dutch role plainly: the form 'reflects the role of the Dutch as chief importers of the leaves in that part of Europe (through the Dutch East India Company, from 1610)'.

nodes.derivation: English tea is first recorded in the 1650s (Pepys, 28 Sept. 1660, spells it tay), borrowed from Dutch thee; the earlier and separate English chaa/cha (1590s) came from Portuguese chá via Macao and represents the other branch of the same Chinese word. Down to the 18th c. tea was pronounced /teː/, rhyming with obey — Pope's Rape of the Lock (1712) rhymes 'tea' with 'obey' — and only later shifted to /tiː/ by the regular Great-Vowel-Shift-era raising of ME/eModE ē. Nourai's Amoy → Malay → Dutch → English chain is the AHD's and the OED's; only Klein interposes French thé instead of Dutch.

entries.modern_form: no reconstructible PIE root; Italian ciarlare / Spanish charlar / Occitan charrar 'to chatter' are independent Romance onomatopoeias
entries.note: The language label is the problem. 'Čar, Char : idle chat' is not an Indo-European root in any modern repertory: it is absent from Pokorny, from Walde-Pokorny and from Watkins/AHD, and every authority that treats the words hanging under it calls them imitative creations of the Romance vernaculars — Klein 'of imitative origin', AHD 'of imitative origin', Etymonline 'echoic', 'perhaps imitative of ducks' quacking'. Pokorny does have expressive/echoic bases in this semantic field (gar- 'rufen, schreien' POK 352, whence Latin garrīre 'to chatter'; ker-² 'echoic root'), but nobody derives ciarlare/charrar from them — Romance onomatopoeias of this shape are formed afresh in each period and are not inherited. Nourai's source is Shipley's Origins of English Words, a book of IE roots that regularly promotes such expressive bases to root status; it could not be consulted (see ref_check). Two further defects: the Italian branch is hung on the wrong peg (Cerreto is a place name from Latin cerrus 'turkey oak', node #1), and the 'French' charra/charrado are Provençal (Occitan), as Nourai's own cited AHD page says (node #5). The individual Romance and English links, taken on their own, are sound.
entries.note_fa: مشکل در برچسب زبانی است. «Čar, Char» به معنای «گپِ بیهوده» در هیچ فهرست امروزی ریشهٔ هندواروپایی نیست: نه در پوکورنی هست، نه در والده‑پوکورنی و نه در واتکینز/AHD؛ و هر مرجعی که واژه‌های زیر این جعبه را بررسی کرده، آن‌ها را ساخته‌هایی آوانمادین (onomatopoeic) در زبان‌های رومی می‌داند — کلاین «of imitative origin»، فرهنگ American Heritage همان، و اتیمانلاین «echoic». درست است که پوکورنی ریشه‌های آوانمادینی در همین حوزهٔ معنایی دارد (gar- «بانگ زدن، فریاد کشیدن»، ص ۳۵۲، که garrīre لاتین از آن است؛ و ker-²)، اما هیچ‌کس ciarlare و charrar را از آن‌ها نمی‌گیرد: آوانماهای رومی از این‌گونه در هر دوره از نو ساخته می‌شوند و ارثی نیستند. مأخذ نورایی کتاب شیپلی است که چنین ستاک‌های آوانمادین را پیوسته به مقام «ریشه» برمی‌کشد و دسترس‌پذیر نبود. دو ایراد دیگر: شاخهٔ ایتالیایی به قلاب نادرست آویخته شده (Cerreto نام جای است، از cerrus لاتین «بلوطِ ترکی») و charra/charrado «فرانسوی» در واقع پرووانسی (اکسیتان) است — چنان‌که خودِ صفحهٔ AHD مورد استناد نورایی می‌گوید. پژوهش امروزی این ریشه را رد می‌کند، هرچند تک‌تک حلقه‌های رومی و انگلیسی به‌خودیِ‌خود درست‌اند.

nodes.derivation: Word by word. (a) Cerreto is a real Umbrian town near Spoleto (today Cerreto di Spoleto), and its name has nothing to do with chatter: it is Latin cerrētum 'oak grove', a collective in -ētum from cerrus 'turkey oak' — so the arrow root('idle chat') → Cerreto is wrong, and this is what makes the node disputed. (b) Cerretano 'man of Cerreto' is the regular Italian ethnic in -ano (cf. romano, napoletano); from the 15th c. the men of Cerreto were licensed alms-collectors for the hospital of Santa Maria della Stella and the word came to mean 'itinerant quack, mountebank'. (c) ciarlatano is cerretano deformed under the pull of ciarlare 'to prattle' (< ciarla 'chatter', imitative) — a textbook contamination, and the reason the two families cross at all. AHD (Nourai's own citation) and Klein both give exactly this; Etymonline and the OED prefer to derive ciarlatano straight from ciarla and treat Cerreto as folk etymology. So Nourai has picked one of the two standard accounts — defensible for ciarlatano, but he has then wrongly made the toponym Cerreto itself a derivative of his chatter root.

nodes.derivation: The etymology is right and the transliteration is wrong. Persian شارلاتان is a 20th-century loan from French charlatan, taken in through the same channel as most European vocabulary in Persian (French-medium schooling and journalism from the late Qajar period); Mo'in and Dehkhoda both tag it [فر.] 'French' and gloss it حقه‌باز، شیاد، کلاهبردار. nodes.derivation: The two forms are real but the language label is off by one: charra 'to chat' and charrado 'chat, long talk' are Provençal (Occitan), not French — as Nourai's own cited page says, AHD deriving charade from 'Provençal charrado, chat, from charra, to chat, chatter'. And since the root box above is not a genuine IE root (see entry note), the arrow into this node cannot be more than an assertion that the word is expressive — which is true, and is all any source claims for it.

nodes.derivation: English charade is first recorded in 1776, borrowed from French charade (itself attested from the 1770s, from Provençal charrado). The original charade was a spoken riddle in which each syllable of a word was described separately and then the whole — the syllable-by-syllable structure is why an 'idle-talk' word could name it. The acted 'dumb charades' developed in the 19th c. and gave the modern party game, normally called by the plural charades, which is the form Nourai's box gives. The chain Provençal → French → English is Klein's, AHD's and Etymonline's alike.

entries.modern_form: Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs) 'sheet/leaf of papyrus, paper'
entries.note: The root, the label and the gloss are all right: Greek χάρτης, masculine, 'sheet of papyrus, paper, book'. Nourai's double headword 'Čartěs, Xartěs' is not two words but his own two transliterations of the one Greek word (he files Greek χ under C so as to keep the English ch- derivatives together, and gives the X-spelling as a cross-reference). Its two branches — east into Aramaic and Arabic, west into Latin — are both real, and between them they account for Persian قرطاس and Persian کارت, which is Nourai's point: the same Greek word reached Persian twice, thirteen centuries apart and from opposite directions. The root box's own note, 'Probably from an Egyptian origin', is the traditional guess and is worth qualifying: Klein says 'a foreign word, possibly of Egypt. origin' and Etymonline 'probably from Egyptian', but Beekes and Chantraine reject the derivation from χαράσσω 'to scratch' and leave the word's origin unknown, while Rendsburg proposes Phoenician ḥrṭyt 'that which has been written' (cf. Biblical Hebrew ḥéreṭ 'stylus'). So: a loanword into Greek, source disputed, Egyptian only one candidate.
entries.note_fa: ریشه و برچسب و معنا هر سه درست‌اند: یونانیِ χάρτης، مذکر، «برگ پاپیروس، کاغذ، کتاب». سرواژهٔ دوگانهٔ «Čartěs, Xartěs» دو واژه نیست بلکه دو آوانگاریِ خودِ نورایی از یک واژهٔ یونانی است (او χ یونانی را ذیل C می‌آورد تا مشتق‌های انگلیسیِ ch‑ کنار هم بمانند و صورت X را همچون ارجاع می‌دهد). هر دو شاخه‌اش — شرقی به آرامی و عربی، غربی به لاتین — حقیقی‌اند و همین دو شاخه‌اند که «قرطاس» و «کارت» فارسی را پدید آورده‌اند؛ و نکتهٔ نورایی هم همین است: یک واژهٔ یونانی دو بار، با فاصلهٔ سیزده سده و از دو سوی مخالف، به فارسی رسیده است. یادداشتِ جعبهٔ ریشه، «احتمالاً خاستگاه مصری»، همان حدسِ سنتی است و باید مقید شود: کلاین می‌نویسد «واژه‌ای بیگانه، شاید مصری» و اتیمانلاین «احتمالاً مصری»، اما بیکس و شانترن اشتقاق آن از χαράσσω «خراشیدن» را رد می‌کنند و خاستگاه را نامعلوم می‌دانند، و رندزبورگ فینیقیِ ḥrṭyt «آنچه نوشته شده» را پیشنهاد می‌کند (سنجیده شود با ḥéreṭ عبریِ کتاب مقدس «قلمِ حکاکی»). پس: وام‌واژه‌ای در یونانی، با خاستگاهی مورد اختلاف، که مصری تنها یکی از نامزدهاست.

nodes.derivation: Arabic قِرْطاس qirṭās 'sheet of papyrus, paper' does come from Greek χάρτης, but not directly: the standard account (Wiktionary, with Dehkhoda agreeing) routes it through Aramaic/Syriac קַרְטִיסָא qarṭīsā, and the form itself shows it — Greek kh- appears as q- and the Greek nominative -ēs is replaced by -ās, both characteristic of the Aramaic mediation that carried most Greek material culture words into pre-Islamic Arabic, rather than of direct Greek→Arabic borrowing. The word is Qur'ānic (VI.7, 'a book on qirṭās'; VI.91, plural qarāṭīs), so the borrowing is pre-Islamic, which fits the Aramaic route through the Christian Arab centres of Syria and Iraq. That is why the verdict is 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed': the source language of the etymon is right, the number of steps is not.

nodes.derivation: Persian قرطاس qerṭās 'paper' is a straight Arabic loan of the classical period, one of the large stock of Arabic writing-trade words that entered New Persian with the Islamic chancery; Mo'in tags it [ع.] 'Arabic' and glosses it کاغذ, with the Arabic broken plural قراطیس qarāṭīs carried over intact. Persian pronounces the Arabic i of qirṭās as e (qerṭās), the regular Iranian treatment of Arabic short i. Nourai's Ferdowsi citation is apt — دبیر جهاندیده را خواند شاه / بیاورد قرطاس و مشک سیاه — and shows the word already naturalised in the Shahnameh (c. 1010 CE) in its literal sense 'writing sheet', paired with مشک سیاه, the lamp-black ink. In Persian it stayed a bookish word: the everyday term was and is کاغذ kāghaz. The ultimate route is Greek → Aramaic → Arabic → Persian, which makes this the eastern of the two paths by which χάρτης reached Persian (compare کارت, node #5).

nodes.derivation: Latin charta 'leaf of papyrus, sheet, document' is an early Latinised borrowing of Greek χάρτης, attested from Cato onwards. Two changes are worth naming. The gender: the Greek word is masculine in -ēs, but Latin made it feminine in -a on the model of its other Greek loans in -a — Ernout–Meillet cite the ancient grammarian Charisius for exactly this rule, and note that Lucilius' masculine cartus (line 709) was an isolated attempt to keep the Greek gender. The spelling: the aspirate is written ch- in the learned form charta but Latin had no /x/, and the plain popular spelling carta — the form that all the Romance languages continue — is the one that prevailed in Late Latin. Nourai's node gives both spellings, which is correct.

nodes.derivation: French carte continues Late Latin carta by the ordinary sound history of the language: intervocalic development is blocked because -rt- is a consonant cluster, so the stem survives intact, and Latin final -a regularly weakens to French -e /ə/. It is attested from the 12th c. in the sense 'written document' and from the 14th c. in the sense that mattered for its diffusion, 'playing card' — Klein and Etymonline both note that the playing-card sense was the oldest in French too. Because French carte is a popular inherited form rather than a learned one, it, and not Latin charta, is the shape that spread across Europe and eventually into Persian (node #5).

nodes.derivation: Persian کارت kārt 'card' is a 20th-century loan from French carte, entering with the European administrative apparatus (کارت ویزیت 'visiting card', کارت شناسایی 'identity card', later کارت ملی, کارت بانکی); Mo'in tags it [فر.] 'French'. French final -e /ə/ is not pronounced, so Persian took the consonant-final stem kārt directly, with ā for the French /a/. The extra form in the box, کارتون kārton, is the same borrowing pattern applied to French carton 'pasteboard' — itself French from Italian cartone, the augmentative of carta — and in Persian it carries both senses, 'cardboard box' and 'animated cartoon'. Together with قرطاس (node #2) this makes Greek χάρτης a doublet in Persian: the same word, once through Aramaic and Arabic in the 10th century, once through Latin and French in the 20th.

nodes.derivation: All five are English via French from Latin charta, and Klein gathers exactly this list under card — but not all five come from the specific French form carte, so the single arrow oversimplifies. card (early 15th c.) is from Old French carte, with an unexplained -t > -d; the sense 'playing card' is the oldest in both languages. chart (1570s) is from French charte 'map, card', the learned doublet of carte, from Latin charta. carton and cartoon are both from French carton 'pasteboard', which is itself from Italian cartone, the augmentative of carta — cartoon entered in the sense 'full-size drawing on stout paper' (an artist's preparatory design) and acquired the comic sense in Punch in the 1840s. cartridge is a corruption of earlier cartrage, from French cartouche 'a roll of paper', from Italian cartoccio, again from carta; Klein's own entry heads it "cartridge, n. — Fr. earlier cartrage, corruption of…". So the node is right that all five descend from Greek χάρτης through Latin and French, and right about card and chart in particular; it is loose in routing carton, cartoon and cartridge through carte rather than through carton and cartouche.

consulted.note: Skeat likewise files all of them under Card: "cartoon … Ital. cartone, lit. a large paper"; "cartouche, cartridge … a roll of paper"; "chart … L. charta, a paper" — same family, different immediate French/Italian donors.
Greek khartēs → Latin charta → Medieval Latin carta → Old French carte → English card.
